transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-03-13
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 49 minutes
Attendees: Evan Morales; Priya Shah; Jon Park; Marta Ruiz — Asha Menon; Diego Navarro; Leah Kim; Tom Becker

Summary:
Quick intake to understand Valebrook's VPC/onramp constraints, preferred private connectivity (peering vs privatelink), region gating for EU data residency, and security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO). Discussed tradeoffs between peering/transit gateway/privatelink for multi-AZ low-latency LLM inference.

Topics covered:
- Current network topology and IP ranges
- AWS Transit Gateway vs VPC Peering vs PrivateLink (Privatelink)
- Egress and NAT gateway cost / bandwidth constraints
- KMS/BYOK and HSM options for key management
- Region restrictions (EU residency + APAC reachability)
- Fallbacks: hosted -> dedicated -> private routing policies

-- Transcript --
[00:00:03] Evan Morales: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick round of intros — i'm evan from Redwood, i handle the account.
[00:00:10] Asha Menon: hi i'm asha, head of infra at valebrook. we own the network and compliance asks.
[00:00:14] Diego Navarro: diego - cloud net eng, i'll be digging into peering and egress.
[00:00:18] Leah Kim: leah, secops, mostly compliance and KMS questions.
[00:00:22] Tom Becker: tom, platform PM, i'll own the rollout plan.
[00:00:25] Priya Shah: priya, solutions eng at redwood, i'll go through the private onramp options.
[00:00:30] Jon Park: jon, solutions as well, i'll touch on perf and KV cache implications.
[00:00:35] Evan Morales: cool. goal for today is to capture constraints and propose next steps. first, can you walk us through your current VPC layout and any region restrictions?
[00:00:45] Asha Menon: sure. primary infra in us-east-1 and eu-west-1. we also have a smaller ap-southeast-1 footprint for local latency to APAC customers. we cannot move eu data outside eu-west-1 for regulatory reasons, so anything that touches eu customer data has to stay in eu.
[00:00:58] Diego Navarro: to add — our VPCs are peered internally through a transit gw, but we have strict egress controls. NAT gateways in each AZ, but we cap bandwidth per account and our finance team is sensitive to high NAT costs.
[00:01:12] Leah Kim: and SOC2 plus a couple european regs — 90 day audit log retention is a minimum, also we may need 2FA on SSO and BYOK for certain workloads.
[00:01:22] Priya Shah: understood. when you say "BYOK", do you mean using your KMS in each cloud region? and HSM for key-wrap?
[00:01:28] Leah Kim: yes BYOK via AWS KMS with CMKs, ideally with external import for HSM-backed wrapping.
[00:01:34] Priya Shah: ok makes sense. two quick architecture options we usually discuss: plain VPC peering/transit (fast, low-latency, but requires route table and IP planning) or AWS PrivateLink/Privatelink style endpoints (more controlled via interface endpoints, less route table complexity, but can add per-GB charges and limited cross-account scaling).
[00:01:52] Diego Navarro: question — we've got limits on how many peering attachments and routes we want to manage. transit gw is already used for other SaaS. can redwood sit behind our transit or do we need per-VPC peering?
[00:02:04] Jon Park: Redwood's private dataplane supports both. we can peer directly or terminate via a transit gw attachment. tradeoff: transit gives centralization but adds an extra hop; peering keeps lowest latency but more config management. also kv-cache locality matters — for small prompt latencies, the extra hop can add 10-30ms depending on path.
[00:02:20] Tom Becker: for our ML workflows, tail latency at 99th percentile matters. can you quantify that 10-30ms impact with a typical gen model?
[00:02:28] Jon Park: rough ballpark for models hosted in-region: peering = baseline. transit attachment adds typically 8-20ms depending on region and whether cross-account NAT is used. if you go cross-region (eu -> us), that's obviously hundreds of ms. for local eu-west-1 fanout, it's small but not negligible.
[00:02:43] Evan Morales: also worth flagging that Redwood supports a fallback policy: if private capacity isn't available we can route to dedicated or hosted endpoints in the same region, but that can change data residency profiles so we only do that with customer agreement and SSO/consent flags.
[00:02:58] Asha Menon: that's critical. we can't accidentally send eu data to us without a legal exception. is that enforced at the routing level?
[00:03:05] Priya Shah: yes we can enforce region-level routing rules and tag-based enforcement. in our private control plane we map customer orgs -> allowed regions. fallback only to pinned compatible variants in the same region unless you opt-in otherwise.
[00:03:16] Leah Kim: about audit logs — do you stream audit events back to our SIEM or do we pull them?
[00:03:22] Jon Park: we have both options. push via Kinesis/Firehose or S3 export with signed access. we can accommodate 90/365 retention windows; the security pack we'll share covers ingestion patterns and sample CloudWatch/CloudTrail mappings.
[00:03:35] Diego Navarro: on networking specifics, what's the preferred pattern for IP whitelisting — do you provide a stable list of egress IPs per region?
[00:03:42] Priya Shah: for private onramp there are two flows: interface endpoints (private link) where traffic stays inside and you don't need whitelisting per se, or peering/transit where you will need to accept routes and possibly whitelist a small CIDR block for control-plane callbacks. we provide a managed set of egress IPs if you need NAT-based egress; those are stable per deployment but you should expect to reserve a handful of IPs.
[00:04:02] Tom Becker: do those egress IPs change during scaling or failover? we want predictable firewall rules.
[00:04:07] Priya Shah: stable across normal autoscaling. during major maintenance/failover there may be a short window but we offer a maintenance calendar and can provide IP ranges well in advance.
[00:04:15] Asha Menon: what about hybrid mix: we want some tenants on private peering and others to use hosted because of cost. can we partition at the tenant or route level?
[00:04:23] Evan Morales: yes. Redwood supports per-route and per-tenant routing policies, so you can direct TTL sensitive or PII-sensitive traffic to private-only endpoints while less-sensitive workloads use hosted. that's part of the routing policy config in the Console.
[00:04:33] Leah Kim: BYOK — does redwood allow us to bring keys and use them for model artifact encryption or just for metadata and audit logs?
[00:04:40] Jon Park: BYOK can be used for data at rest encryption for your customer artifacts and snapshots; model weights (if you host models on Redwood) are encrypted; for inference in the private path we can do end-to-end encryption with your keys for stored artifacts and attested keys for in-flight TLS termination if you require mTLS with client cert validation.
[00:04:59] Diego Navarro: TLS termination — where does it happen in the private path? at your interface endpoint? we prefer to terminate in our VPC if possible.
[00:05:05] Priya Shah: we can support mutual TLS where the TLS is terminated in your VPC (with PrivateLink iface endpoints) or at our side for peering scenarios, with certificate rotation via your KMS. if you want termination in your VPC, we recommend PrivateLink.
[00:05:16] Tom Becker: cost question — PrivateLink has per-GB costs and per-hour ENI charges. our estimate is heavy throughput for inference requests; any guidance on cost-breakpoints?
[00:05:26] Evan Morales: we usually run an analysis: for <X TB/month, peering/transit is often cheaper; for small many-tenant customers with strict security PrivateLink simplifies compliance but can be more expensive at scale. we can run a cost model if you provide QPS, avg token sizes, and expected monthly tokens.
[00:05:40] Asha Menon: here's a question about region gating in APAC — we have users in singapore but a strong policy that european PII can't be sent to APAC. can Redwood restrict model routing by geo for specific datasets?
[00:05:50] Priya Shah: yes that's part of the routing policy layer. you can define routing by dataset flags, tenant attributes, or headers. we also have edge routing where we pin models to a region and deny cross-region fallbacks.
[00:06:00] Leah Kim: around legal/compliance — do you have SOC2 type II and ISO attestation evidence?
[00:06:06] Evan Morales: yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO 27001. we'll share the redacted attestation pack; note some doc names in the pack reference our "RedWood" internal registry (typo in some older PDFs) — apologies for that.
[00:06:17] Diego Navarro: one more nit: how do you handle DNS from our side? split-horizon? we run internal private zones.
[00:06:24] Priya Shah: we can integrate with private hosted zones using conditional forwarders or allow you to host a private zone that the interface endpoint uses. split-horizon is common. we'll include DNS patterns in the network guide.
[00:06:33] Jon Park: socket-level performance note — if you have long-context workloads with heavy KV cache reuse, co-locating inference in the same AZ reduces cache misses and improves overall token latency. that argues for peering or transit attachments inside region AZs rather than cross-AZ PrivateLink egress patterns.
[00:06:50] Tom Becker: are there examples of customers running BYOK + PrivateLink + transit hybrid? we've seen references but want a concrete pattern.
[00:06:57] Priya Shah: yes, a typical pattern: control plane over PrivateLink, data plane over peering/transit, and BYOK for encryption. we'll give a reference architecture doc with diagram — link in next steps.
[00:07:05] Evan Morales: i'd like to capture your immediate blockers — Diego?
[00:07:10] Diego Navarro: we need IP ranges for firewalling, confirmation on whether we need transit attachments per account, and a breakdown of expected egress bandwidth cost. plus, KMS compatibility matrix.
[00:07:20] Leah Kim: from compliance — confirmation that logs can be exported to our SIEM and retention windows supported. and proof points for SOC2.
[00:07:28] Asha Menon: timeline: we want to pilot in eu-west-1 within 6 weeks, then expand to us-east. pilot needs minimal config and predictable failover behavior.
[00:07:36] Evan Morales: ok pilot in 6 weeks is doable. we'll send a checklist and a pilot runbook.
[00:07:40] Jon Park: i'll include perf test scripts — lightweight synthetic loads that exercise KV cache and concurrent streams. we typically run a 24-hour run to surface tail latency.
[00:07:49] Priya Shah: action items and docs we'll share: security pack (SOC2/ISO), private onramp network guide, sample network diagram, perf runbook, cost model template.
[00:07:58] Tom Becker: can you share an enforcement matrix for routing decisions? ie which attributes trigger private-only routing.
[00:08:03] Evan Morales: yes; it's part of the Console policy docs. we'll include a short explainer.
[00:08:08] (background) Speaker 1: mm-hm, okay.
[00:08:12] Diego Navarro: slight tangent — if we ever need on-prem/offline air-gapped inference, what is the path?
[00:08:18] Priya Shah: Redwood has an on-prem package for air-gapped envs; it's more effort and calendar gating but we do it for regulated finance customers. that path typically syncs model bits via signed artifacts and we provide an ops runbook.
[00:08:28] Leah Kim: do you support HSM attestation for key material used in the on-prem case?
[00:08:32] Jon Park: yes, the on-prem deploy can integrate with customer HSMs; our team has done HSM attestation flows with customers.
[00:08:37] Asha Menon: ok, last question — if we start with hosted for a quick MVP and move to private later, how smooth is migration re: model versions and traffic routing?
[00:08:45] Evan Morales: it's designed to be smooth: model versioning and rollout policies are abstracted. you can pin tenants to endpoints and flip a routing flag to move traffic from hosted to private with canary rollouts and automatic fallback. we'll work with you on a migration playbook.
[00:08:59] Tom Becker: perfect.
[00:09:02] Evan Morales: anything else?
[00:09:05] (brief pause)
[00:09:10] Asha Menon: no, thanks. looking forward to the security pack and the transit vs privatelink design notes.
[00:09:15] Evan Morales: great. we'll follow up with materials and schedule the deep-dive. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
